appraisal_events.evidence: « Ils ont si peu rompu que je l'ai trouvée il y a deux jours dans la garçonnière de Robert ; ils n'avaient pas l'air de gens brouillés » — dit par « le prince de Foix qui aimait à répandre tous les bruits pouvant faire manquer un mariage à Robert et qui d'ailleurs pouvait être trompé par les reprises intermittentes d'une liaison en effet finie ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Foix publicly re-attaches Robert to Rachel in front of the salon, damaging his standing as a marriageable man; the narrator's immediate aside exposes the informant's malicious motive and probable error, so the discredit is reported and simultaneously undercut.

appraisal_events.evidence: « c'est une espèce d'évaporée comme vous dites, ce que vous appelez une dégrafée, une sorte de "Dame aux Camélias", au figuré bien entendu » — « Ce discours m'était tenu par le prince Von qui tenait à avoir l'air au courant de la littérature française et des finesses parisiennes ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Von classes Rachel as a loose woman and a courtesan type, lowering her socially; the narrator's closing attribution reframes the verdict as borrowed Parisian chic performed by a foreigner anxious to seem knowing, deflating the speaker along with his judgment.

status_effects.explanation: Robert is locally exposed as still entangled with Rachel and as the object of rumors designed to wreck his marriage, though the narrator's correction limits the damage.
The narrator's aside characterizes Foix as a malicious rumor-spreader who is probably mistaken, discrediting him as an evaluator.
Rachel is spoken of as a demi-mondaine glimpsed in passing on the Champs-Élysées and labelled a "dégrafée" and a "Dame aux Camélias", placing her below the salon that discusses her.
The narrator's final sentence turns Von's worldly verdict into a display of second-hand French literary knowingness, diminishing him rhetorically at the moment he means to shine.

ambiguities: The passage stages a damaging report about Robert and then discredits its source, so it is genuinely double-edged: Robert loses socially through the rumor while the narrator suggests the liaison is in fact over and the rumor malicious.
"le prince de Foix" and "le prince Von" are not on the reference sheet and are recorded with their verbatim surface forms as unresolved.
